docs.title: iVedha Managed Elasticsearch Platform
docs.text:
Deploy Elasticsearch and Kibana from Azure Marketplace into your own Azure subscription, then use supported interfaces to connect data, manage access, and operate the platform with iVedha.

This documentation guides service owners, Azure administrators, network and identity teams, Elastic administrators, and data users from evaluation through day-two operations.

The platform runs in your Azure subscription

You retain ownership of the Azure subscription, infrastructure, data, and Elastic license. iVedha provides and supports the managed service. Opsflw supplies deployment and lifecycle automation. The exact operational scope depends on your approved Marketplace plan and service agreement.

Customers control the Azure subscription, connectivity, identity, and data. iVedha operates the supported platform through Opsflw automation and managed interfaces.

docs.title: What the platform is
docs.text:
The iVedha Managed Elasticsearch Platform is an Azure Managed Application that deploys a pre-engineered Elasticsearch and Kibana environment on Azure Kubernetes Service. Azure creates an application resource for customer-facing status and lifecycle actions and a managed resource group for the supporting platform infrastructure.

The service is intended for teams that need an Elasticsearch platform without designing and operating the entire Azure and Elastic foundation themselves. Depending on the approved service scope, iVedha can manage platform administration, health monitoring, supported upgrades and patching, performance and capacity review, security configuration, troubleshooting, and lifecycle operations.

This is not Elastic Cloud hosted outside your environment. It is also not an unmanaged Kubernetes package that customers must maintain directly. Review the architecture and deployment model and shared responsibility before purchasing or deploying.

docs.text:
Workload Typical outcome Start here Search Index and query application, product, knowledge, or other document collections Onboard search data Observability Collect logs, metrics, traces, and events from applications and infrastructure Onboard observability data Analytics Explore indexed operational or business data with Elasticsearch and Kibana Search and visualize data AI-ready search and operations Use eligible vector, inference, machine-learning, or AI-assisted features after version, license, and configuration checks What AI-ready means

AI-ready does not mean that every AI model or Elastic feature is enabled in every plan. Verify the deployed version, Elastic license, topology, optional machine-learning capacity, connectivity, and data-governance requirements before committing to an AI use case.

docs.text:
Party Primary responsibilities Customer Azure subscription and policy, network connectivity and DNS, Microsoft Entra ID, Elastic licensing, data onboarding, data use, governance, and application-level requirements iVedha Managed-service support and the platform administration, monitoring, maintenance, upgrades, and troubleshooting included in the approved service Opsflw Deployment and lifecycle automation used to provision, configure, and reconcile the managed platform Elastic Elasticsearch and Kibana technology, product behavior, version compatibility, and license-based feature definitions

Customers use the Azure managed application view, Elasticsearch and Kibana interfaces, and documented support actions. Do not modify infrastructure in the managed resource group unless the application explicitly exposes that change.

docs.title: Follow the customer journey
docs.text:
1. Evaluate the service. Review what the platform provides, responsibilities, and support.
  2. Plan the deployment. Confirm Marketplace prerequisites, network design, and profiles and capacity.
  3. Deploy and follow readiness. Use the first-instance tutorial and do not treat Azure acceptance as service readiness.
  4. Connect and secure access. Choose public or private access, verify TLS, and configure users or Microsoft Entra single sign-on.
  5. Onboard production data. Select a supported ingestion path, create least-privilege credentials, and test failure and recovery behavior.
  6. Operate and get support. Monitor health and capacity, use supported maintenance and upgrade workflows, and submit a support request when required.

docs.text:

Before production use, record the deployed versions, approved support scope, recovery objectives, capacity evidence, credential owners, and escalation route. Check compatibility and release notes before adopting a new feature or version.

docs.title: What AI-ready means
docs.text: AI-ready describes the platform's ability to support search and analytics workloads that can use eligible Elastic AI and machine-learning features. It does not mean that every AI feature, model, or external model service is enabled automatically.

docs.title: What the platform provides
docs.text:
Every deployment provides the Elasticsearch and Kibana foundation selected in the Marketplace plan. The deployment form currently distinguishes:

  • a Search profile for full-text, vector, and AI-oriented search workloads;
  • an Observability profile for logs, metrics, and traces;
  • an optional Machine Learning setting.

The selected capacity, topology, Elastic version, license, and managed configuration determine what can be used after deployment.

docs.title: Check feature availability
docs.text:
Capability Availability rule Full-text search and analytics Core Elasticsearch capability; confirm the deployed version Vector fields and vector search Confirm the deployed version and intended index design Elastic machine learning Requires the optional deployment setting and an eligible Elastic license ELSER or other Elastic inference models Use only when the deployed version, license, and model deployment are verified External model providers Requires customer-approved connectivity, credentials, data governance, and a supported integration Kibana AI features Confirm the deployed Kibana version, Elastic license, and managed configuration AI-assisted Opsflw operations Available only when explicitly exposed and approved for the managed application

Do not infer feature availability from the product name or profile label. Check license and feature management and the compatibility reference before designing an AI workload.

docs.title: Responsibility boundary
docs.text:
The customer owns the data, prompts, model-provider agreements, access policy, and use-case governance. iVedha operates the supported platform configuration. Elastic supplies the Elasticsearch and Kibana technology and defines which features belong to each Elastic subscription.

For a workload decision, record:

  1. the required Elastic capability;
  2. the deployment's Elastic version and license;
  3. whether ML or inference capacity is enabled;
  4. required outbound connectivity and credentials;
  5. data classification and model-provider approval;
  6. a representative performance and relevance test.

If any item is unknown, treat the capability as unavailable until it is verified.

docs.title: Limits rule
docs.text: Use limits shown by the approved Marketplace plan, Azure subscription quota, deployed resource configuration, and current Elastic version. Do not copy fixed capacity, retention, availability, or timing values from another deployment.

  • [ ] Required exports and final snapshot are verified.
  • [ ] Dependent DNS, Private Endpoints, identities, and alerts are inventoried.

docs.title: Architecture and deployment model
docs.text: The platform combines Elastic Stack services with Azure infrastructure managed through an Azure Managed Application.

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.text:
The managed platform runs in the customer's Azure subscription. Customers own the subscription, connectivity, identity, and data; iVedha and Opsflw operate the supported platform through managed interfaces.

The diagram is conceptual. The exact Azure resources depend on the approved offer, plan, region, and version. It intentionally omits subnets, node pools, node roles, and internal automation.

docs.title: Service components
docs.text:
• Elasticsearch stores, indexes, and searches data.
  • Kibana provides the browser interface for search, visualizations, dashboards, and supported administration.
  • Azure Kubernetes Service hosts the managed application workloads.
  • Azure Key Vault holds deployment secrets and certificate material.
  • Azure Storage supports deployment data, diagnostics, and snapshot access where configured.
  • Azure networking supplies virtual networks, private connectivity, DNS, and optional public access.
  • Managed identities and Azure RBAC authorize supported communication without embedding Azure credentials in documentation.

Not every underlying resource is intended for direct customer administration. Use the managed application view and documented Elasticsearch or Kibana interfaces for supported changes.

docs.title: Azure resource boundaries
docs.text: Boundary Primary purpose Customer action Application resource group Contains the managed application instance View status and perform supported lifecycle actions Managed resource group Contains supporting infrastructure Inspect only as permitted; do not modify directly Customer network and DNS Connects users and data sources Configure approved routing, DNS, and Private Endpoints Elasticsearch data plane Holds customer indices and configuration Manage data, users, roles, and application-level settings

docs.title: Access models
docs.text:
Private access keeps service endpoints on approved private network paths. Users need a Private Endpoint, working DNS, a trusted TLS certificate, and a route from their client network.

Public access uses internet-reachable endpoints. It still requires TLS, authentication, and any organization-approved network restrictions.

Choose the access model during planning. Changing it later may require DNS, certificate, firewall, and client reconfiguration.

For a focused comparison, see public and private connectivity.

docs.title: Renew TLS certificates
docs.text: Renew certificates before their validity period ends. Keep the old certificate available for controlled rollback until the new certificate is verified.

docs.title: Renew a private certificate
docs.text:
1. Inventory every service hostname and current expiration date.
  2. Generate a new private-scope CSR through the managed application action.
  3. Verify its subject alternative names.
  4. Have the approved certificate authority sign the CSR.
  5. Upload the public leaf and required intermediate certificate chain.
  6. Wait for the managed action to complete.

  7. From each client network, set the exact deployment-provided hostname and verify hostname, chain, and expiration:

    SERVICE_HOSTNAME="<deployment-service-hostname>"

openssl s_client \
  -connect "${SERVICE_HOSTNAME}:443" \
  -servername "${SERVICE_HOSTNAME}" \
  -verify_return_error </dev/null

  8. Confirm the command ends with Verify return code: 0 (ok) and the served certificate has the expected subject alternative name, issuer, serial number, and new expiration date.

  9. Test Kibana sign-in and an Elasticsearch request.
  10. Record the new expiration date and next renewal owner.

Do not upload or distribute the deployment private key. If the certificate is rejected, confirm that it was issued from the current CSR and that the complete chain is present. If clients still receive the old certificate, confirm that the managed action completed and retry from every endpoint and network path before assuming the change propagated.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: The deployed managed application is authoritative for its platform and Elastic versions. Do not select a client, Agent, integration, or feature from the documentation site's publication date.

docs.title: Apply the compatibility rule
docs.text:
Before enabling a feature or changing a component:

  1. record the exact deployed versions;
  2. read the corresponding Elastic compatibility and upgrade guidance;
  3. confirm the feature is exposed by the managed application;
  4. test the change with representative non-production data;
  5. record rollback and support ownership.

The documentation intentionally does not publish an unverified global version matrix. A platform release must add its approved version range here before the release is described as supported.

See release notes for documentation changes and prepare for upgrades for managed upgrade planning.

docs.title: Choose a data onboarding path
docs.text:
Choose an ingestion path only after confirming that its endpoint and component are exposed by your deployment. A URL in source code is not proof that the corresponding service is enabled in your Marketplace plan.

Customers operate the source applications and collection layer. The managed platform receives approved TLS-protected ingestion traffic.

docs.title: Make the onboarding decision
docs.text:
Record:

  1. data owner and classification;
  2. expected events or documents per second and daily volume;
  3. retention and deletion requirements;
  4. approved source and destination network paths;
  5. deployment-derived endpoint and certificate chain;
  6. least-privilege credential owner and rotation interval;
  7. index template, data stream, or integration owner;
  8. failure buffering, retry, and duplicate-handling behavior;
  9. validation queries and dashboards;
  10. support boundary for the source collector or application.

For a complete example, use onboard observability data or onboard search data.

docs.title: Delete the application
docs.text: Deleting the Azure managed application also deletes its managed resource group. Treat deletion as destructive and irreversible unless your recovery plan has been tested.

docs.title: Before deletion
docs.text:
1. Obtain application-owner, data-owner, security, and billing approval.
  2. Stop or redirect ingestion clients.
  3. Export data that must be retained.
  4. Create and verify the required final snapshot.
  5. Confirm where the snapshot is stored and whether deleting the application affects access to it.
  6. Record users, integrations, DNS records, Private Endpoints, certificates, alerts, and dependent applications that must be removed.
  7. Record the managed application resource ID and deletion approval.

docs.title: Delete and monitor
docs.text:
1. In the Azure portal, open the managed application.
  2. Review the resource and managed resource group one final time.
  3. Select the Azure delete action and confirm the exact application.
  4. Monitor the state through Deleting to Deleted.
  5. Do not manually delete individual managed resources to speed up the process.
  6. Escalate if Azure reports deletion failure or managed resources remain after the managed application is gone.

docs.title: Complete decommissioning
docs.text:
• Remove customer-owned Private Endpoints and unused DNS records.
  • Revoke application identities, API keys, and client credentials.
  • Remove monitoring, alerts, allowlists, and integration configuration.
  • Confirm billing and Marketplace subscription state.
  • Retain the approved audit and recovery records without retaining secrets.

Microsoft documents the deletion behavior in Azure Managed Applications overview.

docs.title: Deploy your first platform instance
docs.text: This tutorial follows one non-production example from Marketplace selection to a searchable test document. Replace the fictional values with values approved for your organization.

docs.title: Example choices
docs.text:
Decision Fictional tutorial value Application resource group rg-docs-elastic-demo Workload profile Observability Capacity Small Topology All-in-one Machine learning Disabled Access Public, only when organizational policy permits Public domain Marketplace-assigned default Maintenance window Approved non-business window

The example names are not deployment defaults or recommendations. Use private access instead when internet-reachable endpoints are not approved.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • an approved Marketplace offer and plan;
  • purchasing, deployment, role-assignment, policy, and quota prerequisites;
  • an application resource-group name and approved Azure region;
  • a named network, identity, certificate, data, and support owner;
  • permission to create a disposable synthetic test index.

Complete Marketplace prerequisites and the planning worksheet first.

docs.title: Create the managed application
docs.text:
1. In the Azure portal, open the approved Marketplace offer.
  2. Confirm the publisher is iVedha and the product is iVedha Managed Elasticsearch Platform.
  3. Select the approved plan, then select Create.
  4. On Basics, select the approved subscription, resource group, and region.

  5. Enter an application name that follows your Azure naming policy.

  6. On the deployment profile step, select the approved workload, capacity, topology, and optional ML setting. For this example, use the choices in the preceding table.

  7. Configure the approved private domain. Enable public access only when the security owner approved it. If a custom public domain is enabled, record its DNS owner.

  8. Enter the approved maintenance occurrence, day, start time, time zone, and duration.

  9. Enter the approved support contact.

  10. On Review + create, resolve every validation error and review the configuration, price, terms, permissions, and managed-resource-group settings.

  11. Select Create once the review is correct.

docs.title: Follow the readiness gates
docs.text:
Do not treat Azure acceptance as service readiness:

  1. Wait for Azure to accept the Marketplace request.
  2. Confirm the ARM deployment reports Succeeded.
  3. Open the managed application and wait for its managed reconciliation and health indicators to complete.
  4. Confirm that the Elasticsearch and Kibana URLs appear in the authoritative deployment details.
  5. Complete public or private connectivity, DNS, and TLS.
  6. Open Kibana and confirm an approved user can sign in.

Use follow deployment status for the meaning of each gate and navigate the managed application for the relevant Azure views.

docs.title: Verify with synthetic data
docs.text:
After connectivity and authentication work:

  1. Follow ingest your first data.
  2. Confirm the document is returned by search.
  3. Open Kibana and confirm the data is visible.
  4. Delete the synthetic index.

The instance is ready for handover only after these checks succeed from an approved customer network.

docs.title: Clean up the tutorial instance
docs.text: If the instance is temporary, follow delete the application. Confirm required snapshots, audit records, DNS cleanup, and data-retention decisions before deletion.

docs.title: Deploy the iVedha Managed Elasticsearch Platform
docs.text: Use the exact offer and plan approved by your procurement and platform teams. The available fields can vary by plan, so the deployment form is authoritative for the instance you are creating.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • completed Marketplace prerequisites;
  • approved values from deployment planning;
  • permission to create the managed application and required role assignments;
  • the approved offer link or verified publisher, offer, and plan identity.

docs.title: Create the managed application
docs.text:
1. Sign in to the Azure portal.
  2. Open the approved Marketplace offer.
  3. Verify the publisher is iVedha and the application name is iVedha Managed Elasticsearch Platform.
  4. Select the approved plan, then select Create.
  5. On Basics, select the subscription, application resource group, and region recorded in your planning worksheet.
  6. Complete the workload, capacity, and topology fields shown by the plan.
  7. Select the approved public or private network model. Enter only the domains, network values, contacts, and tags approved for this deployment.
  8. Configure the maintenance, licensing, or identity fields that are present in the selected plan. Do not enter a secret into a free-text or tagging field.
  9. Select Review + create.
  10. Resolve every Azure validation error. Review pricing, terms, permissions, and the managed resource group settings.
  11. Select Create once the review is correct.

docs.title: Confirm Azure accepted the request
docs.text:
Azure should create a deployment record and the managed application resource. Record:

  • subscription and application resource group;
  • managed application resource ID;
  • deployment name and region;
  • selected plan and configuration;
  • deployment operation or correlation ID;
  • creation time.

Azure acceptance does not mean Elasticsearch is ready. Continue with follow deployment status.

Warning

Do not edit resources in the managed resource group while provisioning is in progress. A manual change can be denied or can make the deployment unrecoverable.

docs.title: Deployment fields
docs.text:
The exact fields and allowed values depend on the offer and plan. This reference explains common categories; it does not override the live deployment form.

Category Purpose Evidence to prepare Subscription and region Selects the Azure ownership and location Approved subscription, policy, quota, and region Application identity Names and tags the managed application Naming standard, environment, and ownership tags Workload profile Describes Search or Observability intent Ingestion, search, retention, and user demand Capacity and topology Selects available resource layout Capacity estimate and availability requirement Public access Enables approved public endpoints Exposure approval, DNS owner, domain, and restrictions Private access Enables private service connectivity Client VNet, subnet, routes, DNS, and certificate owner Domain settings Defines customer or managed hostnames Approved DNS zone and certificate names Maintenance Records a controlled change schedule Occurrence, weekday, start time, time zone, duration License Selects or supplies supported licensing Entitlement owner and approved license material Identity or OIDC Configures supported authentication Tenant, application, redirect, claims, and owners Contacts Identifies deployment or support users Approved business email addresses Advanced settings Applies supported expert configuration Product-owner approval and documented validation

Never place a password, private key, access token, or connection string in tags, contacts, advanced YAML, or another field not explicitly designed for a secret.

docs.title: Review deployment outputs
docs.text: Use the managed application's deployment details as the source of truth for resource IDs and endpoint names. Never reconstruct internal resource names from a naming convention.

docs.title: Record the deployment identity
docs.text:
1. In the Azure portal, open Managed applications.
  2. Select the deployed application.
  3. Record the subscription, application resource group, application resource ID, region, and provisioning state.
  4. Open the most recent successful deployment and review Outputs.
  5. Use the managed application view for supported customer-facing properties that are not exposed as ARM outputs.

docs.title: Record connection information
docs.text:
Where present, record:

  • Elasticsearch URL;
  • Kibana URL;
  • Fleet and Logstash URLs if the selected plan exposes them;
  • whether each endpoint is public or private;
  • required service hostnames;
  • the authoritative Private Link Service resource ID;
  • any customer DNS action;
  • certificate or CSR status.

Outputs must not contain secret values. If an output appears to expose a password, token, private key, or connection string, do not copy it into documentation or a ticket. Report it through the approved security process.

docs.title: Verify the outputs
docs.text:
• Hostnames use the approved customer or managed domain.
  • Private endpoints are not expected to work before Private Endpoint, DNS, and TLS configuration is complete.
  • Public endpoints resolve to the expected public path and present a trusted certificate.
  • The recorded Private Link Service resource ID comes directly from deployment details.

Next, choose an access model.

docs.title: Follow deployment status
docs.text: Check the managed application and its Azure deployment operations while the platform completes provisioning and readiness checks.

docs.title: Customer-visible lifecycle
docs.text:
State Meaning Your action Accepted Azure accepted the create request Wait and monitor deployment operations Succeeded Azure completed the resource deployment Continue waiting until service readiness is confirmed Failed Azure or a downstream readiness step failed Preserve evidence and follow deployment troubleshooting Deleting Azure accepted deletion Do not recreate resources with the same identity Deleted The application and managed resource group are gone Confirm required records and data-retention actions

Azure resource deployment success and application readiness are separate milestones. Elasticsearch, Kibana, networking, certificates, and managed automation can require additional reconciliation after ARM reports success.

Azure resource success is one gate in the managed-platform lifecycle, not the final readiness signal.

docs.title: Readiness gates
docs.text: Gate Evidence Complete when Marketplace accepted Azure create request Azure created a deployment record ARM succeeded Resource-group deployment All required ARM operations succeeded Managed reconciliation complete Health and Sync Status The managed application reports the desired state Service ready Elasticsearch and Kibana health Customer-facing services report healthy Endpoints published Deployment outputs or properties Authoritative URLs and identifiers are present Customer connectivity ready Client-side checks Network, DNS, TLS, and authentication work Handover complete Recorded validation Owners accept access, monitoring, support, and recovery

docs.title: Monitor progress
docs.text:
1. In the Azure portal, open Managed applications.
  2. Select the application and review its provisioning state.
  3. Open the application resource group and review Deployments.
  4. If a deployment is active, wait rather than starting a duplicate.
  5. When Azure reports success, use the managed application view or approved deployment details to confirm endpoints and platform health.
  6. Record the first time at which the application is ready for customer use.

docs.title: When to escalate
docs.text:
Escalate when:

  • Azure reports Failed;
  • progress stops and no deployment operation is active;
  • the managed application is successful but no authoritative endpoints appear;
  • the service remains unavailable after the documented readiness process.

Include the safe evidence listed in troubleshoot deployment problems. Do not include tokens, passwords, private keys, or unredacted deployment parameter values.

docs.title: Choose an access model
docs.text:
Start with the access model recorded in the deployment outputs.

Public access uses public DNS and a TLS-protected endpoint. Private access requires a customer route, private DNS answer, Private Endpoint, and Private Link path.

docs.title: Public access
docs.text:
Use configure public access when the deployment exposes internet-reachable URLs. You still need:

  • authoritative public DNS;
  • a certificate valid for each service hostname;
  • approved network restrictions;
  • Elasticsearch authentication and authorization.

docs.title: Private access
docs.text:
Complete these procedures in order:

  1. Create a Private Endpoint to supply the network path.
  2. Configure private DNS so service hostnames resolve to the Private Endpoint.
  3. Configure private TLS so clients can verify the service hostname and certificate chain.
  4. Sign in securely.

Each layer solves a different problem:

Layer Successful result Private Endpoint and routing TCP traffic reaches the deployment privately DNS The service hostname resolves to the endpoint's private IP TLS The certificate matches the hostname and chains to a trusted CA Authentication Elasticsearch or Kibana accepts the user or client

Do not troubleshoot authentication until connectivity, DNS, and TLS work. Do not use an IP address in place of the service hostname.

docs.title: Follow the private request path
docs.text: Troubleshoot private access in order: route and endpoint, DNS, TCP 443, Private Link, TLS, and authentication.

docs.title: Get support
docs.text:
Use Request Support in the deployed managed application or the contact shown in its approved Marketplace listing. A source-code portal URL or internal channel is not an approved customer support route unless it appears there.

Keep one support record from initial impact through customer-validated closure.

docs.title: Submit through the managed application
docs.text:
1. Open the managed application Overview.
  2. Select Request Support.
  3. Enter Your Email Address.
  4. Enter a concise Request Subject.
  5. In Request Description, state the impact, start time, affected users or services, exact symptom, and troubleshooting already completed.
  6. Review the form for credentials, personal data, and customer content.
  7. Submit the request and retain the resulting reference.

docs.title: Classify the impact
docs.text:
Use the severity term defined in the approved Marketplace support agreement. If the agreement uses P1–P4, classify impact consistently:

Severity Customer impact example P1 critical Production service unavailable, widespread data ingestion stopped, or active security impact with no workaround P2 high Major production function degraded or a material group blocked with no acceptable workaround P3 medium Limited degradation, non-critical function affected, or an acceptable workaround exists P4 low Information request, documentation question, or planned change guidance

This table helps describe impact; it does not create a response-time commitment. Support hours, initial-response targets, escalation intervals, and service exclusions come from the approved offer or service agreement.

docs.title: Include
docs.text:
• managed application resource ID;
  • subscription and application resource group names when approved for sharing;
  • deployment region and plan;
  • problem start time and time zone;
  • exact user-visible symptom;
  • affected endpoint or operation without credentials;
  • whether one or all users and networks are affected;
  • last known successful time;
  • Azure deployment or correlation ID;
  • redacted error code and message;
  • diagnostic steps already completed;
  • business impact and required response time.

Use this subject pattern:

[P1-P4] <application name> - <region> - <short symptom>

Use this description structure:

Impact:
Started:
Last known good:
Affected users, sources, or endpoints:
Observed error:
Expected result:
Recent approved change:
Checks completed:
Correlation or deployment ID:
Safe attachment list:
Contact and time zone:

docs.title: Do not include
docs.text:
• passwords, one-time passwords, API keys, tokens, cookies, or headers;
  • private keys or complete certificate bundles;
  • unredacted ARM parameters or environment dumps;
  • customer documents, indexed records, or personal information;
  • credential-bearing Git remotes or internal automation endpoints.

If the issue is an Azure purchasing, subscription, policy, or platform-service problem rather than application behavior, use the Azure support path approved by your organization.

docs.title: Escalation and communications
docs.text:
• Use the ticket reference for updates; do not split one incident across unapproved channels.
  • State immediately when impact or scope increases.
  • Ask for an escalation through the support route when the response target in the approved agreement is missed.
  • Record maintenance, workaround, recovery, and closure decisions.
  • For a suspected credential or data exposure, use the approved security incident route rather than attaching sensitive evidence to a normal ticket.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Application resource group Customer-controlled resource group containing the managed application   resource. Azure Managed Application Azure resource that packages a supported application and its managed   infrastructure. Elasticsearch Distributed search and analytics engine that indexes and queries data. Kibana Elastic user interface for exploring, visualizing, and administering data and   supported cluster features. Managed resource group Resource group containing application infrastructure governed by the managed   application definition. Private Endpoint Customer-owned network interface that gives a service a private IP in a VNet. Private Link Service Service-side Azure resource to which an approved Private Endpoint connects. Private DNS DNS namespace visible to approved private networks that maps service   hostnames to private endpoint addresses. Snapshot Elasticsearch backup stored in an off-cluster snapshot repository. Subject alternative name Certificate field listing the hostnames for which the certificate is valid. TLS Protocol that encrypts a connection and verifies service identity through a   certificate and trust chain.

docs.title: Monitor health and capacity
docs.text: Monitor both customer workloads and managed-service readiness. A green Azure resource state does not prove that ingestion, search, or every Elasticsearch index is healthy.

docs.title: Review cluster health
docs.text:
With an appropriately privileged user:

curl --fail-with-body --user "<user>" \
  "https://<elasticsearch-hostname>/_cluster/health?pretty"

Review:

  • cluster status and unassigned shards;
  • node availability;
  • disk use and growth;
  • indexing rejection or latency;
  • search latency and errors;
  • shard count and size;
  • snapshot failures;
  • Kibana and client availability.

docs.title: Respond to disk pressure
docs.text:
Elasticsearch uses disk watermarks to protect nodes. At the flood-stage watermark it can block writes to affected indices. Do not permanently raise watermarks to hide insufficient capacity.

  1. Confirm which nodes and indices are affected.
  2. Stop avoidable ingestion bursts.
  3. Delete data only under an approved retention decision.
  4. Request a supported capacity or topology change when growth is durable.
  5. Confirm that write blocks clear and ingestion recovers.

See Elastic watermark errors for current product behavior.

docs.title: Request a capacity change
docs.text: Provide current capacity, observed growth, retention, peak ingestion, query load, shard metrics, business deadline, and the requested outcome. Do not ask for a size label without supporting workload evidence.

docs.title: Ingest your first data
docs.text: Use a non-production test index and a user that can create and read that index. Do not paste production secrets or sensitive data into a tutorial request.

docs.title: Create a test document
docs.text:
1. Confirm that you can reach the Elasticsearch URL.

  2. Set the endpoint without including credentials:

    export ELASTICSEARCH_URL="https://<elasticsearch-hostname>"

  3. Index one synthetic document:

    curl --fail-with-body --user "<user>" \
  --request POST \
  "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/docs-validation/_doc?refresh=wait_for" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "@timestamp": "2026-07-28T00:00:00Z",
    "message": "documentation validation event",
    "environment": "test"
  }'

  4. Enter the password through the client prompt or an approved secret mechanism.

  5. Confirm that the response reports a successful create or update result.

docs.title: Search for the document
docs.text:
curl --fail-with-body --user "<user>" \
  "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/docs-validation/_search?q=environment:test"

Confirm that the response contains the validation event.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
Delete the test index after validation:

curl --fail-with-body --user "<user>" \
  --request DELETE \
  "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/docs-validation"

If the request is rejected, verify the user's index privileges. Do not solve a permission error by giving the user broad cluster-administrator access.

For production use, choose a data onboarding path, then follow the observability or search tutorial. Validate every selected integration against the deployed Elastic version.

docs.title: What is the iVedha Managed Elasticsearch Platform?
docs.text:
The iVedha Managed Elasticsearch Platform is an Azure Managed Application that deploys Elasticsearch and Kibana with supporting Azure infrastructure in your Azure subscription.

It is intended for teams that want to use Elasticsearch for search, observability, or analytics without designing the underlying Azure platform from the beginning.

iVedha provides and supports the managed service. Opsflw supplies deployment and lifecycle automation. Elasticsearch and Kibana are Elastic technologies deployed in the customer's Azure subscription.

docs.title: What you receive
docs.text:
A deployment can include:

  • Elasticsearch for indexing, search, and analytics;
  • Kibana for data exploration, visualization, and administration;
  • Azure networking and private connectivity;
  • managed identities, Key Vault, storage, and operational logging;
  • deployment lifecycle and maintenance automation.

The exact resources, topology, capacity, endpoints, and licensed features depend on the plan and options shown in your approved Marketplace offer.

The platform is AI-ready, not AI-by-default. Review what AI-ready means before selecting an AI, vector search, inference, or machine-learning use case.

docs.title: How Azure manages the application
docs.text:
Azure represents the service as a managed application. The application resource is in a resource group that you control. Supporting resources are placed in a managed resource group. Access to that group is governed by the managed application definition and may be restricted.

Do not change resources in the managed resource group unless the application explicitly exposes the action. Uncoordinated changes can be denied or can prevent iVedha from supporting the deployment.

docs.title: Start safely
docs.text:
1. Review the shared-responsibility model.
  2. Confirm Marketplace prerequisites.
  3. Complete the deployment planning worksheet.
  4. Follow the deployment guide.

For the Azure platform model, see Azure Managed Applications overview.

docs.title: Manage the Elastic license
docs.text: Elastic features depend on the active license and deployment configuration. The source package supports Basic, trial, and supplied commercial-license paths, but the options available to you depend on the approved offer and plan.

docs.title: Check license status
docs.text:
Use an authorized account:

curl --fail-with-body --user "<user>" \
  "https://<elasticsearch-hostname>/_license"

Record the license type, status, and expiration when present. Do not copy a license file or credential into a ticket.

docs.title: Change license configuration
docs.text:
1. Confirm the commercial entitlement and the features that require it.
  2. Confirm that the managed application exposes a license action.
  3. Store the supplied license material only through that protected action.
  4. Submit the change and wait for it to complete.
  5. Recheck the Elasticsearch license API.
  6. Test one required licensed feature with a least-privilege account.

Do not install an undocumented command-line tool, place license material in source control, or infer a license from the Marketplace plan name.

If the action is unavailable or the license is rejected, preserve the API status and error text after removing sensitive values, then get support.

docs.title: Lifecycle states
docs.text:
State Customer meaning Terminal? Accepted Azure accepted the requested lifecycle action No Succeeded Azure completed the reported resource action Not necessarily service-ready Failed The current create or delete episode failed Yes for that episode Deleting Deprovisioning is active No Deleted The managed application is absent Yes

The managed service can continue readiness checks after ARM reports Succeeded. Treat the application as ready only when authoritative endpoints, health, access, and the documented readiness result are available.

Repeated or delayed events are an implementation concern, not a reason for a customer to create duplicate applications or edit managed resources.

See follow deployment status for the customer procedure.

docs.title: Manage maintenance
docs.text: The deployment can record a maintenance schedule for coordinated platform changes. Use the managed application action only when it is available for the deployed plan.

docs.title: Prepare for maintenance
docs.text:
1. Confirm the occurrence, weekday, start time, time zone, and duration shown by the deployment.
  2. Identify affected users, ingestion pipelines, and client retry behavior.
  3. Review service health and active incidents.
  4. Verify a recent usable snapshot when the change can affect data.
  5. Communicate the expected impact through approved channels.

docs.title: Update the schedule
docs.text:
1. Open the managed application in the Azure portal.
  2. Open the supported maintenance configuration action.
  3. Enter the approved schedule and time zone.
  4. Review the value carefully; do not infer local time from UTC.
  5. Submit the change and record its operation or change identifier.
  6. Wait for the action to complete before submitting another schedule change.

docs.title: Validate afterward
docs.text:
• Elasticsearch cluster health is acceptable.
  • Kibana loads and users can authenticate.
  • Ingestion and searches have recovered.
  • No unexpected certificate, DNS, or license warning is present.
  • The managed application shows the intended schedule.

If the maintenance action is missing, the schedule does not update, or service health degrades, collect safe evidence and get support.

docs.title: Navigate the managed application
docs.text: The Azure Managed Application is the customer-facing control point for deployment details and supported lifecycle actions. Available commands can vary by offer, plan, and application version.

docs.title: Open the application
docs.text:
1. In the Azure portal, search for Managed applications.
  2. Select the application in its application resource group.
  3. Confirm the application name, subscription, resource group, location, and provisioning state.
  4. Use JSON View when you need the complete managed application resource ID. Copy the id value; do not reconstruct it.

docs.title: Use overview actions
docs.text:
The current source package defines these overview actions. Use an action only when it appears in the deployed application:

Action Outcome Certificate Management Download a private or public CSR and upload the corresponding signed public certificate chain DNS Management Open deployment-specific DNS configuration guidance Request Support Submit an email, subject, and problem description for the managed application

An action that is absent is not available for that deployment. Do not modify managed infrastructure to reproduce it.

docs.title: Review My Deployment
docs.text:
Under Resources, open My Deployment. The current source package defines columns for:

  • Deployment Name;
  • Application;
  • Profile;
  • Capacity;
  • Topology;
  • Location;
  • Health;
  • Sync Status;
  • More Info.

Do not infer readiness from one column alone. Azure provisioning, platform health, synchronization, endpoint publication, and customer connectivity are separate gates.

docs.title: Configure supported settings
docs.text:
When Configure Deployment is available, it can expose controlled changes for profile, network and DNS, maintenance, licensing, OIDC, and advanced configuration. Only enable a change after recording its owner, expected impact, maintenance requirement, rollback path, and validation steps.

Never place a client secret, license payload, private key, or advanced configuration in a screenshot or support ticket.

docs.title: Find endpoints and outputs
docs.text: Use the latest successful deployment's Outputs and customer-facing properties to find the deployment-provided URLs and domains. Continue with review deployment outputs.

docs.title: Marketplace prerequisites
docs.text: Complete these checks with your Azure billing, subscription, identity, and network administrators before opening the deployment form.

docs.title: Marketplace and billing
docs.text:
1. Confirm that Microsoft Marketplace purchases are enabled for the billing account and subscription.
  2. Confirm that the deploying user may purchase or accept the approved offer.
  3. If your organization uses Private Marketplace, confirm that the offer and plan are allowed.
  4. Use the offer link or offer identity approved by your procurement team. Do not choose a similarly named listing.

Microsoft documents the current purchasing controls in Enable Marketplace purchases.

docs.title: Azure access
docs.text:
The deploying identity needs permission to create a managed application and its application resource group. Additional permissions can be required by your organization's policy, networking, role-assignment, or delegated identity model.

Do not assume that an Azure Contributor role can create every required role assignment. Ask an Azure administrator to validate the deployment against your tenant's RBAC and policy design.

docs.title: Subscription readiness
docs.text:
Confirm:

  • the target subscription and Microsoft Entra tenant;
  • the approved Azure region;
  • sufficient compute, storage, networking, and public IP quota for the chosen deployment;
  • required Azure resource providers are registered;
  • Azure Policy permits the resource types and selected region;
  • naming and tagging requirements;
  • a resource group for the managed application;
  • customer contacts who can receive deployment and support communication.

docs.title: Network decision
docs.text:
Choose public or private access before deployment. For private access, identify the client VNet, subnet, routing owner, DNS owner, and certificate authority.

Record the approved values in the deployment planning worksheet.

docs.title: Network design
docs.text: Network design determines whether users and data sources can reach the service. Finalize it before deployment to avoid address, route, DNS, and certificate rework.

docs.title: Choose the access model
docs.text:
Use private access when clients must remain on private Azure, peered, VPN-connected, or ExpressRoute-connected networks. Use public access only when internet-reachable endpoints are allowed by your security policy.

Authentication and TLS are required in both models.

docs.title: Private-access checklist
docs.text:
• Client and platform address spaces do not overlap.
  • The Private Endpoint subnet has available addresses.
  • Network policy permits a Private Endpoint in that subnet.
  • A route exists from every client network to the endpoint.
  • The DNS design covers Azure-native and hybrid clients.
  • The DNS owner can create the required records or forwarding rules.
  • The certificate authority can issue a certificate for the deployment hostnames.
  • Firewalls permit only required client-to-service connections.

docs.title: Public-access checklist
docs.text:
• Internet exposure is approved.
  • The authoritative public DNS owner is identified.
  • The selected domain and certificate names match.
  • Source restrictions or proxy controls are documented.
  • Users will still authenticate with individual accounts.

docs.title: Separate the failure domains
docs.text:
Troubleshoot in this order:

  1. Routing and Private Endpoint provide the network path.
  2. DNS maps the service hostname to the intended endpoint.
  3. TLS verifies the hostname and certificate trust.
  4. Authentication verifies the user or client.

Do not replace a service hostname with an IP address to bypass DNS. The TLS certificate is issued for hostnames, not for an arbitrary endpoint IP.

docs.title: Onboard observability data
docs.text:
Use an OpenTelemetry Collector in gateway mode so applications send to a customer-operated collector that can batch, retry, and control egress. This procedure applies only when the deployment's Elasticsearch version supports the OTLP/HTTP endpoint.

Applications send telemetry to a customer-operated Collector. The Collector uses the deployment-provided HTTPS endpoint; telemetry remains in the customer's Azure-hosted managed platform.

docs.title: Choose the supported intake path
docs.text:
Do not treat all Elastic OpenTelemetry endpoints as interchangeable:

Path When to use it Direct Elasticsearch OTLP/HTTP Use this tutorial only after confirming the deployed Elasticsearch version exposes /_otlp/v1/logs, /_otlp/v1/metrics, and /_otlp/v1/traces Customer-operated Collector Recommended gateway for batching, retry, egress control, and limiting application connection churn APM Server OTLP intake Use only when the deployment explicitly exposes and supports an APM Server endpoint; its protocol and paths differ Elastic Agent and Fleet Use when Fleet and the required integration are exposed and compatible with the deployed Elastic version

The direct Elasticsearch endpoint accepts OTLP/HTTP with protobuf encoding. It does not accept OTLP/gRPC. Do not send OTLP to Kibana, omit the /_otlp base path, or guess that a Cloud-hosted or APM endpoint exists.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Confirm:

  • the deployment-derived Elasticsearch URL;
  • OTLP/HTTP support for the deployed version;
  • TCP 443, DNS, and TLS trust from the collector;
  • an administrator who can create a scoped API key;
  • a non-production source for the first validation;
  • ownership for collector availability, buffering, and upgrades.

docs.title: Create a least-privilege API key
docs.text:
Set the endpoint without credentials:

export ELASTICSEARCH_URL="https://<deployment-elasticsearch-hostname>"

Using an approved administrator credential, create an expiring onboarding key:

curl --fail-with-body --user "<api-key-administrator>" \
  --request POST "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/_security/api_key" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "name": "otel-gateway",
    "expiration": "30d",
    "role_descriptors": {
      "otel_writer": {
        "indices": [
          {
            "names": ["logs-*", "metrics-*", "traces-*"],
            "privileges": ["auto_configure", "create_doc"]
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  }'

Enter the administrator password through the client prompt. Store the returned encoded API key in the approved secret store; do not place it in a file, screenshot, shell history, or ticket.

docs.title: Configure the Collector
docs.text:
Use environment substitution for the endpoint and secret:

receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      http:

processors:
  batch: {}
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_mib: 512

exporters:
  otlphttp/elastic:
    endpoint: ${env:ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/_otlp
    headers:
      Authorization: "ApiKey ${env:ELASTIC_API_KEY}"

service:
  pipelines:
    logs:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch]
      exporters: [otlphttp/elastic]
    metrics:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch]
      exporters: [otlphttp/elastic]
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch]
      exporters: [otlphttp/elastic]

Pin a Collector version supported by your organization. Add persistent buffering, high availability, resource limits, and telemetry for the Collector before production use.

The exporter appends /v1/logs, /v1/metrics, or /v1/traces to the /_otlp base path. Follow the Elastic Elasticsearch OTLP/HTTP endpoint guidance for the deployed version rather than copying configuration for Elastic Cloud Managed OTLP or APM Server.

docs.title: Verify and hand over
docs.text:
1. Send one synthetic log, metric, and trace from a test source.
  2. Confirm the Collector reports successful export without retry or TLS errors.
  3. In Kibana, confirm logs-*, metrics-*, and traces-* data streams appear only for the signals sent.
  4. Verify timestamps, service identity, environment, and sensitive-field handling.
  5. Test Collector restart and destination unavailability behavior.
  6. Record the API-key owner and rotation date.

Revoke the test key if the onboarding is abandoned. For endpoint or TLS failures, follow connectivity troubleshooting.

docs.title: Onboard search data
docs.text: This tutorial creates a synthetic docs-search-default data stream. Use a separate naming, mapping, lifecycle, and relevance design for production data.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • the deployment-derived Elasticsearch URL;
  • working DNS and TLS;
  • an administrator with permission to create index templates and API keys;
  • approval to create and delete tutorial resources.

Set the endpoint without embedding credentials:

export ELASTICSEARCH_URL="https://<deployment-elasticsearch-hostname>"

docs.title: Create the data-stream template
docs.text:
curl --fail-with-body --user "<search-administrator>" \
  --request PUT "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/_index_template/docs-search-template" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "index_patterns": ["docs-search-*"],
    "data_stream": {},
    "template": {
      "mappings": {
        "properties": {
          "@timestamp": {"type": "date"},
          "title": {"type": "text"},
          "body": {"type": "text"},
          "source_id": {"type": "keyword"}
        }
      }
    }
  }'

Confirm the response contains "acknowledged":true.

docs.title: Create the writer API key
docs.text:
curl --fail-with-body --user "<api-key-administrator>" \
  --request POST "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/_security/api_key" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "name": "docs-search-writer",
    "expiration": "7d",
    "role_descriptors": {
      "docs_search_writer": {
        "indices": [
          {
            "names": ["docs-search-*"],
            "privileges": ["auto_configure", "create_doc"]
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  }'

Confirm that the response contains an API-key ID and encoded key. Store both in the approved secret store.

docs.title: Create the validation API key
docs.text:
Use a separate read-only identity for the tutorial search:

curl --fail-with-body --user "<api-key-administrator>" \
  --request POST "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/_security/api_key" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "name": "docs-search-validator",
    "expiration": "7d",
    "role_descriptors": {
      "docs_search_validator": {
        "indices": [
          {
            "names": ["docs-search-*"],
            "privileges": ["read"]
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  }'

Store the validation key and its ID separately from the writer key. A production ingestion identity normally does not need read.

docs.title: Load the keys without echoing them
docs.text:
Retrieve the encoded values from the approved secret store and enter them at the prompts:

IFS= read -rsp "Writer API key: " ELASTIC_WRITE_API_KEY
printf "\n"
IFS= read -rsp "Validation API key: " ELASTIC_READ_API_KEY
printf "\n"

The secret input is not echoed and is not part of the command stored in Bash history. Do not export either variable, save it in a shell profile, or enter the value directly on a command line.

docs.title: Index and search a document
docs.text:
curl --fail-with-body \
  --request POST \
  "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/docs-search-default/_doc?op_type=create&refresh=wait_for" \
  --header "Authorization: ApiKey ${ELASTIC_WRITE_API_KEY}" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "@timestamp": "2026-07-29T00:00:00Z",
    "title": "Synthetic onboarding document",
    "body": "This document validates the managed search ingestion path.",
    "source_id": "docs-tutorial-001"
  }'

Confirm the response reports "result":"created", then search:

curl --fail-with-body \
  "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/docs-search-default/_search?q=source_id:docs-tutorial-001" \
  --header "Authorization: ApiKey ${ELASTIC_READ_API_KEY}"

The response must contain exactly the synthetic document. Remove the keys from the current shell immediately after validation:

unset ELASTIC_WRITE_API_KEY ELASTIC_READ_API_KEY

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
Delete the tutorial data stream and template with an approved administrator, then invalidate the API key:

curl --fail-with-body --user "<search-administrator>" \
  --request DELETE "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/_data_stream/docs-search-default"

curl --fail-with-body --user "<search-administrator>" \
  --request DELETE "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/_index_template/docs-search-template"

Use both API-key IDs returned at creation time with the invalidate API. Do not reuse either tutorial key for production.

docs.title: Operations overview
docs.text: Use the managed application view, Elasticsearch and Kibana product interfaces, and approved support actions. Do not modify the managed infrastructure directly.

docs.title: Daily
docs.text:
• Check service availability and important ingestion failures.
  • Review cluster health and capacity alerts.
  • Investigate authentication or certificate warnings.

docs.title: Weekly
docs.text:
• Review data growth, shard health, query performance, and failed jobs.
  • Confirm that snapshot operations are succeeding where configured.
  • Review open deployment or support actions.

docs.title: Before a planned change
docs.text:
• Confirm ownership, scope, risk, validation, rollback, and maintenance timing.
  • Take or verify a usable snapshot when the change can affect data.
  • Test access with a non-administrator account after the change.

docs.title: Supported tasks
docs.text:
• Monitor health and capacity
  • Manage maintenance
  • Manage the Elastic license
  • Back up and restore
  • Prepare for upgrades
  • Renew TLS certificates
  • Delete the application

Record customer-visible changes and their validation results. Never place passwords, access tokens, private keys, or unredacted diagnostics in the change record.

docs.title: Deployment planning
docs.text: Complete this worksheet before starting the Marketplace deployment. Use values approved by the owning Azure teams; do not invent or reconstruct them.

docs.title: Application and ownership

• Azure subscription and tenant:

  • Azure region:

  • Billing and application owner:
  • Primary technical contact:

docs.title: Workload
docs.text:
• Primary use case: search, observability, analytics, or mixed:
  • Expected daily ingestion:
  • Expected searchable data:
  • Retention objective:
  • Availability objective:
  • Recovery point and recovery time objectives:
  • Expected concurrent users and query pattern:

Use these inputs to select only the profiles and options shown in the approved offer. Do not interpret a profile label as a capacity guarantee; review its displayed resource definition.

• Access model: public or private:
  • Client networks:
  • Client VNet and Private Endpoint subnet:
  • Routing or peering owner:
  • DNS authority:
  • Private DNS or conditional-forwarding owner:

docs.text:
• Elasticsearch administrators:
  • User and role approval owner:
  • Single sign-on requirement:
  • License source and owner:
  • Maintenance window and time zone:
  • Snapshot and recovery-test owner:
  • Azure monitoring and support-evidence owner:
  • Decommissioning approver:

docs.title: Readiness decision
docs.text: Proceed only when Marketplace access, quota, policy, networking, identity, and ownership are confirmed. Resolve unknown deployment-specific values with the owning team or iVedha support rather than copying values from another environment.

docs.title: Create a Private Endpoint
docs.text: A Private Endpoint places a network interface with a private IP in a customer subnet and connects it to the deployment's Private Link Service.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • the authoritative Private Link Service resource ID from deployment outputs;
  • permission to create a Private Endpoint in the selected resource group and subnet;
  • an approved VNet and subnet with available address space;
  • a route from the intended client networks.

Warning

Never reconstruct the Private Link Service resource ID from a resource-name pattern. Internal Azure names can change. Use the value from deployment details or obtain it from iVedha support.

docs.title: Create the endpoint
docs.text:
1. In the Azure portal, search for Private endpoints.
  2. Select Create.
  3. On Basics, choose the subscription and resource group that will own the endpoint. Enter an approved name and region.
  4. On Resource, choose the option to connect by resource ID or alias.
  5. Paste the complete Private Link Service resource ID from deployment details.
  6. On Virtual Network, select the approved VNet and subnet.
  7. Configure application security groups or tags only when required by your organization.
  8. Review the settings and select Create.

docs.title: Confirm connection approval
docs.text:
1. Open the created Private Endpoint.
  2. Check Connection status.
  3. If it is Pending, ask the owner shown in deployment details or iVedha support to review the request. Same-subscription requests are not guaranteed to be automatically approved.
  4. Continue only when the status is Approved.

Record the endpoint resource ID, network interface, private IP, subnet, and approval time. Do not publish these deployment-specific values.

The endpoint does not configure application DNS or TLS. Continue with configure private DNS.

docs.title: Configure private DNS
docs.text: Private DNS maps each service hostname to the Private Endpoint's private IP. Use the exact hostnames and private domain from deployment details.

docs.title: Gather authoritative values
docs.text:
Record:

  • Elasticsearch, Kibana, and any other private service hostnames;
  • the Private Endpoint private IP;
  • the VNet from which clients query DNS;
  • the authoritative private DNS zone or corporate DNS owner.

Do not assume a privatelink.* zone name. This application can use a deployment-specific private domain.

docs.title: Azure-native DNS
docs.text:
1. Create or select the Azure Private DNS zone that is authoritative for the deployment's private domain.
  2. Link the zone to every VNet whose clients must resolve the names.
  3. For each hostname supplied by the deployment, create the required record pointing to the Private Endpoint IP. Derive the record label from the authoritative hostname, not from an internal resource name.
  4. Disable VM autoregistration unless the zone has a separate documented need for it.

  5. Query each hostname from a client in a linked VNet:

    nslookup <service-hostname>

  6. Confirm the response is the Private Endpoint's private IP.

docs.title: Hybrid DNS
docs.text:
For on-premises or custom-DNS clients:

  1. Keep the Azure Private DNS zone linked to the endpoint VNet.
  2. Configure a supported Azure DNS forwarding path, such as Azure DNS Private Resolver, from the corporate DNS service.
  3. Add a conditional forwarder for the deployment's private domain.
  4. Test from both an Azure client and an on-premises client.

Do not forward on-premises queries directly to Azure's platform virtual IP. Use a supported resolver reachable from the client network.

docs.title: Validate the result
docs.text:
DNS is complete when every documented service hostname resolves to the private IP from every approved client network. If it returns NXDOMAIN, a public IP, or an old private IP, follow connectivity troubleshooting.

Next, configure private TLS.

docs.title: Configure private TLS
docs.text:
For a customer-owned private domain, the customer certificate authority must issue the certificate. The supported workflow uses the deployment-generated private key and certificate signing request (CSR).

The private key remains in the managed platform. The customer exchanges only the CSR and signed public certificate chain.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • working Private Endpoint connectivity;
  • working private DNS;
  • the exact private service hostnames;
  • access to the certificate or CSR action exposed by the managed application;
  • a certificate authority trusted by every client.

docs.title: Issue and upload the certificate
docs.text:
1. In the managed application view, open the approved private-certificate action.
  2. Download the private-scope CSR.
  3. Inspect the CSR and confirm that its subject alternative names cover every private service hostname supplied by the deployment.
  4. Submit the CSR to the approved certificate authority.
  5. Obtain the issued leaf certificate and required intermediate certificates in the format accepted by the upload action.
  6. Upload the public certificate chain through the private-certificate action.
  7. Wait until the action reports completion and the endpoint serves the new certificate.

Do not upload or send a private key. The deployment retains the private key used to create the CSR and validates that the returned certificate matches it.

docs.title: Verify TLS
docs.text:
From an approved client, set the exact deployment-provided hostname:

SERVICE_HOSTNAME="<deployment-service-hostname>"

openssl s_client \
  -connect "${SERVICE_HOSTNAME}:443" \
  -servername "${SERVICE_HOSTNAME}" \
  -verify_return_error </dev/null

Confirm:

  • the command ends with Verify return code: 0 (ok);
  • the certificate is within its validity period;
  • the hostname appears in the subject alternative names;
  • the chain ends at a CA trusted by the client;
  • no private key or secret appears in command output saved for support.

Name or service not known indicates DNS failure. Connection timed out or Connection refused indicates a network or endpoint failure. unable to get local issuer certificate indicates an incomplete or untrusted chain. certificate verify failed requires inspection of the detailed verification error; do not disable verification.

Repeat the check for each service hostname. Then sign in securely.

docs.title: Profiles and capacity
docs.text:
The Marketplace form can expose workload, capacity, topology, and optional feature choices. The available combinations depend on the approved offer and plan.

The current Marketplace source defines the following planning choices. Confirm that the same labels and descriptions appear in the approved live offer before using them.

docs.title: Workload profiles
docs.text: Profile Marketplace intent Planning evidence to collect Observability Logs, metrics, and traces Daily ingest, event size, retention, query patterns, dashboards, and concurrent users Search Full-text, vector, and AI-oriented search Document count and size, update rate, query mix, latency target, relevance tests, and vector dimensions

docs.title: Capacity profiles
docs.text:
Capacity Marketplace planning range Interpretation Small Up to 100 GB/day ingest and up to 2 TB stored Starting range for lighter workloads Medium 100–500 GB/day ingest and up to 10 TB stored Starting range for growing workloads Large At least 500 GB/day ingest and more than 10 TB stored Starting range for heavy workloads

These are planning ranges from the source definition, not performance, retention, cost, or service-level guarantees. Validate a representative workload before production.

docs.title: Topology choices
docs.text:
Topology Source-defined purpose Availability All-in-one A high-availability-ready layout without data tiering Search and Observability Master/data Dedicated master and data roles for balanced scale Search and Observability Master/hot/warm Dedicated masters with hot and warm data tiers Observability in the current source definition Optional ML Adds machine-learning capability when selected Requires deployment support and an eligible Elastic license

Node counts, Azure VM sizes, JVM heap, usable disk, replica policy, availability-zone placement, and horizontal scale increments are not published until the runtime configuration and live offer are verified.

docs.title: Require a versioned sizing record
docs.text:
Before approving a production profile, obtain a sizing record for the exact Marketplace plan and platform release. It must include:

Required value Why it matters Platform and Elastic versions Connects the sizing statement to a reproducible release Elasticsearch instance count and roles Establishes the physical topology behind the profile label AKS node-pool VM size and count Identifies the Azure compute consumed by the platform CPU, memory, and Elasticsearch JVM heap Supports workload and concurrency review Disk per instance and usable storage after replicas Prevents treating raw disk as customer-usable capacity Example daily ingest and retention assumptions Explains the workload model used for planning Baseline availability and placement Supports resilience and recovery review Horizontal scale increment Shows the operational effect of a capacity change Azure infrastructure-cost estimate and assumptions Supports commercial review in the customer's region Limits and excluded workloads Prevents unsupported use of a general size label

If the seller, approved offer, or service schedule does not provide these values, treat the physical sizing and cost as unresolved. The Small, Medium, and Large ranges alone are not enough for production approval.

docs.title: All-in-one
docs.text: All-in-one keeps Elasticsearch roles together. The three instances illustrate the source-defined minimum description, not a capacity guarantee.

docs.title: Dedicated master and data
docs.text: The master/data topology separates cluster coordination from data and query workloads.

docs.title: Dedicated master, hot, and warm
docs.text: The hot/warm topology separates active and historical data tiers. Lifecycle movement and retention still require an approved policy.

docs.title: Select a profile
docs.text:
1. Start with measured or estimated ingestion, retention, query, and user requirements.
  2. Review the resources and limitations displayed for each available choice.
  3. Confirm that the topology meets your availability requirements.
  4. Confirm that licensed features required by the workload are available.
  5. Validate the choice with representative ingest and query tests.
  6. Record the selected values and the evidence used for the decision.

docs.title: Avoid unsupported assumptions
docs.text:
• A size label is not a service-level objective.
  • Retention is not automatically implied by a topology.
  • Machine learning availability depends on both deployment configuration and the Elastic license.
  • A capacity change can affect cost, maintenance, and performance.

After deployment, monitor actual ingestion, shard count, disk use, query latency, and growth. Use health and capacity before requesting a profile change.

docs.title: Configure public access
docs.text: Use this procedure only when the deployment outputs identify public service URLs and your security policy permits public access.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Obtain from deployment details:

  • every public service hostname;
  • the authoritative DNS target or records requested by the deployment;
  • certificate status;
  • any approved source restrictions.

Do not invent an IP address or infer a target from an internal Azure resource.

docs.title: Configure and verify DNS
docs.text:
1. Ask the authoritative DNS owner to create exactly the records supplied by the deployment.
  2. Wait for the record's configured DNS time to live.

  3. From an approved client, query each hostname:

    nslookup <service-hostname>

  4. Confirm the answer matches the authoritative deployment target.

  5. Open the Kibana URL by hostname and confirm that the browser trusts the certificate.

  6. Test the Elasticsearch URL without placing credentials on the command line:

    curl --fail-with-body --user "<user>" \
  "https://<elasticsearch-hostname>/"

    Enter the password when prompted by the client or use an organization- approved secret mechanism.

docs.title: Safe result
docs.text:
DNS resolves consistently, TLS has no hostname or trust error, and the service returns an authentication response or authenticated product response.

If the hostname does not resolve, verify the authoritative record. If it resolves but the connection fails, follow connectivity troubleshooting.

docs.text:

  • managed actions and endpoints;
